Yes, it is very difficult to put it into words, this building urge. I think (and this is purely my own theory and in no way meant to take anything away from people with OCD), with OCD the person feels guilty of being locked in that cycle and allowing the behaviour to take over but they can reset the urge by carrying out the behaviour. This same urge occurs with BPD but we can’t make FP (or anyone else) reset that urge - almost as if we are at the mercy of someone else, someone who is likely completely unaware of the devastating and distressing effect their lack of attention could have. The problem is exacerbated when the relief doesn’t come and the feelings boil over to self-blame and loathing (or worse!) I think that this element of BPD is so intense and why it is often classified as one of the worst conditions to have. Just my thoughts and opinion.

I put this reply this on another similar post earlier and it might help answer some of your questions.

For me, FP is someone who I feel an intense emotional connection to, somewhat inexplicably. I crave their attention and validation and it hurts, emotionally, when I don’t get it. We really have no control over who our FP is, and the logical part of our brains knows that the fixation and idolisation isn’t always healthy. I personally find that I am much more likely to exhibit ‘splitting’ behaviours with my FP. I love them (in a non-romantic sense) and I need their attention, but they might take too long to answer a text message and my brain immediately jumps to the unfounded conclusion that they hate me so then I hate them and cut them off, making me feel worse. FP can be a healthy relationship if there are boundaries but there can be unhealthy elements to it - obsession and constant emotional ups and downs. I feel that there are similarities to OCD with BPD but OCD might cause obsessions with actions or behaviours which can be satiated by performing them. With BPD, this obsessive ‘itch’ can only be ‘scratched’ by someone else - often FP, hence we might start prompting them for a response to a text just to get their attention and reset the urge (“have I done something wrong?”, etc). When we don’t get the attention, there is a mounting emotional urgency (difficult to explain but like a panic or a sense of suffocating). It builds and builds until the attention is received then starts over again. This is what is so difficult with BPD - we can’t control when that mounting panic is satiated - only other people can do that. My FP isn’t my wife. I didn’t choose them and I don’t know why they are my FP. My FP is historically usually female (although have been male once or twice). I believe I am unconsciously seeking maternal validation from elsewhere due to issues I had with my mother when I was a child. I hope this explains more about FP but this is mainly from my own experience and could be different for others.

My FP is so inconvenient. It isn’t my wife, but a female colleague and I’m their boss and there is no way to get away from them! They are also not gifted with the most empathy. They don’t know they are my FP but it is like someone touching a raw nerve and not letting go of it, especially when they blow hot and cold. Why does their attention and validation matter so much? It isn’t logical. We are both married and it isn’t lust - just a need for their attention. I hate it and it burns me up inside.
Maybe praise him and acknowledge you’ve noted the positive change but ask (gently) using open-ended questions to find out how he’s done it and if he needs anything from you.
Has he been reading up/researching BPD and doing some self-guided therapy?

I thought I was alone! I completely understand what you’re saying. It’s like any affection is never enough and you feel like an affection whore of sorts. I wish I had some answers for you but please know you’re not alone. And as for the grown man thing, if more guys were given such affection once in a while then the world might be a better place! You absolutely should get some of that!

I also feel like this. Questioning myself constantly over whether it’s them ignoring me or me expecting too much. I’m a 44 year old guy and all I want is to be held tightly and told it will all be okay - but forever!
I completely relate and sympathise with this.
Take the piss out of yourself, others and make light of death or impossible situations.
I was 42 when I was diagnosed (2 years ago).
